extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, designing, and using informal and formal research methods in public relations practice, including surveys, content analysis, social media monitoring, and field intelligence. Emphasizes matching methods to research questions and using research across planning, monitoring, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online community networks (virtual focus groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create social networks of selected “representatives” to respond to questions, consider proposals, try procedures, or use products in development; groups can include hundreds or thousands of participants and different panels can be kept for different issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exploratory, informal information-gathering approach because questions remain about how representative these groups and the social-network experience are of the real world. Use for issue identification and pretesting program strategies prior to formal testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community forums and public meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use public meetings, hearings, town halls, and required community engagement meetings to solicit information and participation from citizens and stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek community input early and often to remain responsive; however, experimental evidence cited indicates that sincere power sharing (true sharing of decision authority) increases satisfaction more than the timing (early vs late). Recognize the varying nature of engagement (see types of participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of community engagement (participation spectrum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of community engagement: (1) Pseudo‑participation — meetings held but input not intended to be factored in; (2) Information‑only — simply informing the public and possibly attaching input to reports; (3) Consultation — soliciting input that may affect final design; (4) Full participation — collaborating and sharing decision‑making so community ideas are incorporated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which type is being offered; misrepresenting engagement (pseudo participation) backfires. Design engagement level to match organizational willingness to act on input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory committees and boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing committees/boards used as continuous feedback mechanisms for long-running programs and issues, tapping expertise and providing regular input on public opinion and program design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only appoint committees when the motivation is sincere; advice must be given earnest consideration and organizations must be prepared to act on input. Committees supplement but do not substitute for formal representative methods; they are exploratory and useful for increasing interaction and probing issues in depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ombudsman / ombuds officer role and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: An ombuds officer listens to concerns of internal publics, reviews policies, mediates disputes, and can investigate organizational problems and recommend remedial action; roles vary from truly independent investigators to facilitators who protect bureaucracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the ombudsman's scope and authority — independent authority to act distinguishes effective ombudsmen from those who only create an illusion of responsiveness. Recognize self‑selection bias: information from ombuds programs reflects those who seek help and may not represent broader publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call‑in telephone lines (hotlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Toll‑free numbers provide instant feedback and allow monitoring of public concerns and reactions; can be used for consumers, employees, patients, and citizens navigating bureaucracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be effective, hotlines must be used with sincerity and actively monitored — failing to act on calls undermines credibility. Beware of SLOP (self‑selected listener opinion poll) bias: call data detect issues but cannot substitute for measuring frequency or distribution of opinions across stakeholder groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mail and email analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic analysis of incoming traditional mail and email to identify areas of favor/disfavor, information needs, and early warnings of ill will or problem relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter writers tend to be critical rather than complimentary and represent a self‑selected sample. Use mail/email analyses as early warning signals and code correspondence for trends, but do not treat them as representative measures of public opinion without further formal research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media and online monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor the Internet — search engines, chat rooms, forums, blogs, and social media — to detect what is being said about an organization and to prevent or manage cybercrises and rumor spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monitoring tools and services (e.g., Google, Bing, Cision, Radian6) to 'harvest' online comments and track buzz. Recognize limitations: online comments are informal, publics are hard to identify, and such monitoring cannot produce representative profiles of public opinion; use it for detection and to join conversations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field reports (district agents, field representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train district agents and field reps to observe and report regularly; they act as the organization's eyes and ears in their territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide easy, regular reporting mechanisms and train staff to listen and observe. Be cautious of reporting bias ('gild the lily') and self‑preservation tendencies — field reports are subjective and best used as early warning signals that may prompt formal investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal research methods (general principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal methods gather data from entire populations (census) or scientifically representative samples using objective measures; they allow descriptions within established accuracy/tolerance and enable inferential statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly determine research questions and objectives before selecting design; avoid focusing on technique at the expense of usefulness. Formal methods are essential for making accurate statements about publics and for basing program design and evaluation on evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research design decision checklist (eight core questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight questions to answer when designing research: (1) What information is needed and why? (2) What publics should be targeted? (3) When are findings needed? (4) How will findings be used? (5) What is the most appropriate research method? (6) How will findings be summarized and interpreted? (7) When and to whom will findings be presented? (8) Who is responsible for ensuring findings are used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to align research design with decision needs and timing; consult the flowchart (Figure 11.3) for project design sequencing. Ensuring answers before selecting methods increases usefulness and likelihood of findings being applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary analysis and online databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuse existing data collected by others (secondary analysis) and search governmental, commercial, academic, and media databases (e.g., Census, LexisNexis, Dun & Bradstreet, Dow Jones) for relevant information and trend data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before conducting new research, check whether others have already done relevant work; secondary data can be far less costly than new data collection and may be segmented by geography or demographics. Use online databases for access to news, market research, financial reports, and government records, but note commercial services may require fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic procedures for objectively determining what is being reported in media (newspapers, TV, websites, blogs, books, advertising, journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content analysis differs from unsystematic scanning by focusing on representativeness of sampled content and objective coding procedures. It measures media placement of messages and can forecast public agenda items, but it does not measure audience exposure, understanding, or belief (impact). Use content analysis for trend detection and issue‑tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys (core adequacy criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys are systematic queries of subsets of a population and can be administered by mail, in person, telephone, or online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey adequacy depends on sampling procedures, question design, and administration mode. Choose administration and sampling to match research goals and be aware of mode‑specific biases and limitations (see mailed, in‑person, telephone, online entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailed surveys: advantages and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mailed questionnaires save time/money, offer respondent convenience and anonymity, and standardize wording with no interviewer bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major disadvantage is low and potentially biased response rates — a random initial sample may become unrepresentative by nonresponse. Other issues: lack of control over who responds, inability to clarify questions, and difficulties in maintaining current mailing lists. Do not assume conventional response rate thresholds (e.g., 50%) guarantee representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: In‑person (face‑to‑face) surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Face‑to‑face administration can yield higher response rates, flexibility, control over conditions, and observation of reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disadvantages include higher costs, possible respondent bias when facing an interviewer, inconvenience, reduced anonymity, and difficulty reaching selected cases. Interviewer influence is a key risk; therefore, interviewer training is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone surveys and sampling challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Telephone interviews are faster and more cost‑effective with some anonymity; challenges include incomplete listings, cell‑phone only households, answering machines, caller ID, and declining working numbers dialed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods like random digit dialing (RDD) and technological aids (CATI) to improve sampling. Be aware of rising costs and sampling difficulties; CATI and IVR variations can offer routing and convenience but have their own limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online surveys: advantages and sampling limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Online questionnaires offer convenience, efficiency, and automated data tabulation; templates and services (e.g., surveymonkey.com) simplify survey creation for practitioners with little formal training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major challenges are obtaining adequate sampling frames (email lists) and low response rates due to filtering and junk mail. Organizations that maintain e‑mail lists can productively use online surveys; otherwise, exercise caution about representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑sectional vs. panel and trend surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross‑section surveys sample a population at a single point in time; panel studies survey the same respondents repeatedly; trend studies use different samples from the same population over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use panel studies to track individual change but expect panel mortality (dropout) and sensitization (respondents become more attentive). Use trend studies to track distributions over time while avoiding panel problems, but note inability to attribute changes to specific individuals. Choose design based on whether change over time or distribution tracking is the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research across program lifecycle and consistent measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Research initiates, monitors, and concludes the problem‑solving process — it defines the problem, provides benchmark data, monitors progress, and evaluates program effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure methods and measures used in evaluation are the same as those used in problem definition to allow valid before/after comparisons. Combine research findings with experience and judgment to design effective public relations programs.
